name: Vosseparkje
title: Ancient Trees in Vosseparkje, Leeuwarden: 7 Worth Finding
meta_description: A pocket park built in 1872 around a reservoir, now holding seven registered trees: a leaning acacia, two feather elms and an unidentified oak.
intro: Vosseparkje, officially Westerpark, exists because Leeuwarden needed a reservoir more than it needed a park. Garden architect Gerrit Vlaskamp landscaped the grounds around the city's drinking-water works in 1872, and the park he drew was redesigned once more in 1926, by which point most of its oldest trees were already decades in the ground. Seven of them sit on the Dutch national monument register today, all inside a few minutes' walk of each other. A Caucasian wingnut from the Caspian forests carries a trunk over a metre round and a scar from a 1987 ice storm. A black locust planted in 1924 has spent a century leaning and is now held up by a prop. Two feather elms of the same narrow cultivar stand at opposite ends of the park, told apart by which one is nearer the pond, and an oak by the south-east entrance has stumped the register itself: its own entry reads Caucasian or Persian oak, undecided, and nobody has settled which. Free, open, no ticket.
